newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO aims for central role in new Europe.
newsitem.headline: NATO aims for central role in new Europe.

text.p: The two great European conflicts of the 20th century were followed by peace settlements blamed for sowing the seeds of a new confrontation.
With a historic NATO-Russia pact now clinched, the Western allies are confident an emerging post-Cold War security arrangement will be a case of third time lucky.

The deal with Moscow outlining a new political and military relationship allows the U.S.-led North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) to proceed with plans for its eastwards expansion into former communist Europe.

In return, Moscow gets a permanent voice at the centre of Europe's security order which critics say its diminished status no longer merits and which it will misuse to undermine the rights of smaller nations.
"Either way, NATO -- the Cold War victor -- is to change beyond recognition," said one diplomat.
Proponents say both the pact and enlargement will allow the most powerful defence organisation ever created to secure a future as continental Europe's main guarantor of stability in the 21st century.

Pessimists led by former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger say the move risks destroying the world's most successful military alliance and once again selling out the interests of small states to Europe's Great Powers.
"Kissinger argues it is a matter of letting the fox into the hen-house and that view has quite a lot of support in Congress," said one NATO official.

U.S. President Bill Clinton hailed the pact with Russia as "an historic step closer to a peaceful, undivided, democratic Europe." President Boris Yeltsin said it eased Russia's fears that NATO's expansion would threaten its security.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, a determined advocate of closer integration of Russia in Western institutions, telephoned Yeltsin to express his satisfaction with the deal.
The "Founding Act on Mutual Relations, Cooperation and Security between NATO and the Russian Federation" is set to be signed by Yeltsin and the 16 NATO leaders in Paris on May 27.

The 16-page pact -- struck by NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Moscow on Tuesday -- creates a NATO-Russia permanent council to be based at NATO's headquarters In Brussels.
Less than two months after it is adopted, the NATO allies will meet in Madrid on July 8-9 to invite at least Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the alliance.
Romania and Slovenia are lobbying hard to join, but the mechanics of bringing five new states at the same time into an organisation which operates by consensus counts against them.
"There are problems, such as meeting rooms, car park space, in addition to the argument that says only the most ready should get in," said one source.

Diplomats say a limited enlargement will right the wrongs of the Yalta conference at the end of World War Two when most of eastern Europe was left to come under the "zone of influence" of Josef Stalin's Soviet Union.

The allies say Russia needed to be brought into the emerging settlement for the aspirations of other states to be met, avoiding the mistake of the Versailles settlement of World War One when the victors' tough terms created tensions later.

NATO countries intend to try and answer the concerns of applicants left out of enlargement by creating a new Atlantic Partnership Council which will link alliance members and partnership countries in one organisation.
The current Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme will be relaunched with plans for increased military cooperation and joint military exercises between all states.

NATO diplomats say such moves could go a long way towards settling the nerves of countries, such as the three Baltic states, which have little hope of alliance membership and most suspicion of Russia.
"Together the Atlantic Partnership Council, an enhanced PFP, the NATO-Russia Council and enlargement should ensure a security system protecting shared democratic values," added the diplomat.
